title: Bans aren’t the answer
author: Emily Freitag
summary: Emily Freitag, who has observed AI-powered products in about a thousand classrooms, argues that AI in schools is neither simply good nor bad but a source of power that can be used for great or harmful ends. Her tour found that the biggest risk to learning came from Google Search's AI Overview, which students copied without reading, and that bans in large districts did not remove it. Bans did, however, appear to rule out helpful uses such as AI-assisted writing practice and feedback and speech-recognition tools that pinpoint letter sounds struggled with by early readers. She warns that regulating AI as a category is a quagmire because it is hard to define and is being built into everything. Drawing on the history of electricity, she urges policymakers to act quickly on safety and privacy but to build a framework for watching real classroom use before regulating instruction.
points: The biggest risk to learning she saw came from Google Search AI Overviews that students copied unread, a tool few people call AI and one that school bans did not remove.
Bans can block valuable uses, such as AI tools that give students far more writing practice and feedback than any teacher could deliver, and speech-recognition tools that target letter-sound gaps.
Regulating by whether AI is present is unworkable because AI is hard to define and is increasingly embedded in every kind of technology.
Policy should focus on the jobs a tool is doing (practice and feedback yes, spiritual counsel no) and on how well it does them.
The electricity analogy suggests acting fast on safety and privacy while setting up structures for leaders to observe real classroom use before regulating instruction.
quotes: AI is both a huge opportunity for learning and a huge risk to learning at the same time. AI in schools is not one thing; it is a source of power to do many things—some great, some horrible.
But I did regularly see students open their search browser, ask a question, and copy the “AI Overview” summary without questioning it or—as far as I could tell—usually even reading it.

I have seen screenshots of computers in New York and L.A. (where most AI is banned in K–12 schools) that show the AI summary in Google Search still alive and active. The bans do not seem to have ruled out the biggest risk to learning I saw on the tour.

I saw targeted instructional tools use AI to give students massively more practice and feedback on their writing than the most industrious human teacher could deliver in a week. It didn’t eliminate the need for teachers to also read and provide feedback on student work, but it did give teachers a huge assist in a laborious instructional job.

It is hard to come to a consensus definition about what AI even is. Even if you could get large groups of people to agree on definitions, the technology is changing so rapidly that they’d need near-constant revision.
I want the very best technology available to help my kids get practice and get feedback on writing, but I don’t want any technology giving them spiritual counsel.
Policymakers should act quickly on what we know about safety and data privacy, but when it comes to instruction, we have a lot more to learn before we know how to regulate.
